introduction.p: The area between two curves can be computed by adding thin strips. For vertical strips, the height is the upper function minus the lower function; for horizontal strips, the width is the right boundary minus the left boundary. Split the region where the order of the boundaries changes.

The order matters. Area is positive. The height of a vertical strip is top minus bottom, not bottom minus top.

exercise.title: Why is the small piece top minus bottom?

statement.p: Area under one graph used height above the axis. Area between two graphs uses g(x)-f(x). In your own words, why is the thickness of a vertical strip the difference of the two boundary values, and why does the order of subtraction matter?

hint.p: Ordinary area is positive. The height of a strip is the upper boundary minus the lower boundary, not the other way around.

exercise.title: Why can you not skip the picture?

statement.p: The curves y=x and y=x^3 switch which graph is on top at an intersection. In your own words, why does integrating a single difference over the whole interval fail, and why are intersections places where the description of the region may change?

hint.p: A definite integral cancels negative contributions. Ordinary area does not. Split wherever top and bottom trade places.

subsection.p: Area between curves is still area. We have only replaced a rectangle under one curve by a strip between two curves. The next step changes dimension. A strip becomes a slice.

exercise.title: What stays the same when the boundary is measured rather than given by a formula?

statement.p: A table of shoreline distances still leads to an approximate integral of strip heights. In your own words, why does missing a formula change how we estimate the integral, but not what the integral means?

hint.p: The small piece is still measured strip height times strip width. Data only change the method of adding those pieces.
